evidence_contexts.source_text: ## The Matrix Factorization Model
Matrix Factorization :cite:`Koren.Bell.Volinsky.2009` is a well-established algorithm in the recommender systems literature.
Latent factor models such as matrix factorization are examples of model-based CF.
Although the final score was the result of an ensemble solution (i.e., a combination of many algorithms), the matrix factorization algorithm played a critical role in the final blend.

The first version of matrix factorization model is proposed by Simon Funk in a famous [blog
post](https://sifter.org/~simon/journal/20061211.html) in which he described the idea of factorizing the interaction matrix.
In this section, we will dive into the details of the matrix factorization model and its implementation.
This computation is important in an area called matrix factorization.
# Matrix Factorization

\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{MSE} (\hat{\theta}_n, \theta) &= E[(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta)^2] \\
 &= E[(\hat{\theta}_n)^2] + E[\theta^2] - 2E[\hat{\theta}_n\theta] \\
 &= \mathrm{Var} [\hat{\theta}_n] + E[\hat{\theta}_n]^2 + \mathrm{Var} [\theta] + E[\theta]^2 - 2E[\hat{\theta}_n]E[\theta] \\
 &= (E[\hat{\theta}_n] - E[\theta])^2 + \mathrm{Var} [\hat{\theta}_n] + \mathrm{Var} [\theta] \\
 &= (E[\hat{\theta}_n - \theta])^2 + \mathrm{Var} [\hat{\theta}_n] + \mathrm{Var} [\theta] \\
 &= (\mathrm{bias} [\hat{\theta}_n])^2 + \mathrm{Var} (\hat{\theta}_n) + \mathrm{Var} [\theta].\\
\end{aligned}
$$

evidence_contexts.source_text: At the current scale, the object detection model needs to predict the classes and offsets of $hw$ sets of anchor boxes on the input image, where different sets have different centers.
* Single shot multibox detection is a multiscale object detection model.

In a nutshell,
via its base network and several multiscale feature map blocks,
single-shot multibox detection
generates a varying number of anchor boxes with different sizes,
and detects varying-size objects
by predicting classes and offsets
of these anchor boxes (thus the bounding boxes);
thus, this is a multiscale object detection model.

For a predicted bounding box $B$,
the object detection model calculates the predicted likelihood
for each class.

Now we are ready to use such background
knowledge to design an object detection model:
single shot multibox detection
(SSD) :cite:`Liu.Anguelov.Erhan.ea.2016`.

We will design an object detection model
based on anchor boxes in :numref:`sec_ssd`.

In order to train an object detection model,
we need *class* and *offset* labels for each anchor box,
where the former is
the class of the object relevant to the anchor box
and the latter is the offset
of the ground-truth bounding box relative to the anchor box.

![As a multiscale object detection model, single-shot multibox detection mainly consists of a base network followed by several multiscale feature map blocks.](../img/ssd.svg)
:label:`fig_ssd`
Synthetic: Object detection is the task, while an object detection model is the trained network that performs it.

proposed_definition_en: a model that detects objects in an image by predicting their classes and locations.

evidence_contexts.source_text:
CNN-based architectures are now ubiquitous
in the field of computer vision, 
and have become so dominant
that hardly anyone today would develop
a commercial application or enter a competition
related to image recognition, object detection,
or semantic segmentation,
without building off of this approach.

# Semantic Segmentation and the Dataset
:label:`sec_semantic_segmentation`
Next, we will show how to use *fully convolutional networks* for semantic segmentation of images.

Since deep neural networks can effectively represent images in multiple levels, 
such layerwise representations have been successfully 
used in various computer vision tasks such as *object detection*, *semantic segmentation*, and *style transfer*.

Different from object detection,
semantic segmentation
recognizes and understands
what are in images in pixel level:
its labeling and prediction of semantic regions are
in pixel level.

:numref:`fig_segmentation` shows the labels
of the dog, cat, and background of the image in semantic segmentation.

This section will discuss the problem of *semantic segmentation*,
which focuses on how to divide an image into regions belonging to different semantic classes.

Compared with in object detection,
the pixel-level borders labeled
in semantic segmentation are obviously more fine-grained.
Synthetic: Semantic segmentation labels every pixel, whereas object detection only draws boxes around objects.

proposed_definition_en: the computer vision task of assigning semantic class labels to image regions or pixels

evidence_contexts.source_text:
The nonvolitional cue is based on
the saliency and conspicuity of objects in the environment.

As shown in :numref:`fig_qkv`,
we can design attention pooling
so that the given query (volitional cue) can interact with keys (nonvolitional cues),
which guides bias selection over values (sensory inputs).

To begin with, consider the simpler case where only
nonvolitional cues are available.

![Using the nonvolitional cue based on saliency (red cup, non-paper), attention is involuntarily directed to the coffee.](../img/eye-coffee.svg)
:width:`400px`
:label:`fig_eye-coffee`

![Attention mechanisms bias selection over values (sensory inputs) via attention pooling, which incorporates queries (volitional cues) and keys (nonvolitional cues).](../img/qkv.svg)
:label:`fig_qkv`

More generally,
every value is paired with a *key*,
which can be thought of the nonvolitional cue of that sensory input.

In this framework,
subjects selectively direct the spotlight of attention
using both the *nonvolitional cue* and *volitional cue*.
* Attention mechanisms bias selection over values (sensory inputs) via attention pooling, which incorporates queries (volitional cues) and keys (nonvolitional cues).
Synthetic: In psychology, a nonvolitional cue can pull attention to a bright object even when the observer intends to look elsewhere.

proposed_definition_en: an attention cue arising automatically from salient sensory input rather than deliberate intention
